label: Java Backend (Fresher)
blurb: Java backend interview prep for 0–2 YOE: core Java, OOP, collections, Spring Boot basics, SQL, REST APIs, DSA, Git, and behavioral questions that come up in fresher and first-job interviews.
audience: 0–2 YOE Java developers, fresh graduates, bootcamp completers

modules.title: Java Syntax & Language Fundamentals
modules.intro: Java syntax interview questions are the first thing every interviewer reaches for when screening a fresher. This module covers the building blocks of the Java language — primitive vs reference data types, how Java handles type casting (widening vs narrowing), every category of operator (arithmetic, bitwise, logical, ternary), control-flow constructs (if/else, switch, for, while, enhanced for-loop), and single-dimensional arrays. The access modifiers (public, private, protected, default) come up in every OOP discussion, so they are covered here before the dedicated OOP module. Each answer is written for someone who has been coding in Java for less than a year: Java jargon is defined on first use, every code block is a complete runnable program with a public static void main entry point, and every answer closes with 'what the interviewer is really checking' so you understand the meta-signal behind the question.

modules.title: Java OOP Fundamentals
modules.intro: OOP interview questions are the single most common opener in any Java fresher interview. Every interviewer will ask you to explain the four pillars — encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction — and then probe with a follow-up that tests whether you understand the concept or just memorised the definition. This module covers: what a class and object actually are in memory, how encapsulation hides state (getters/setters, why private fields), how inheritance works with the extends keyword and method overriding, the two forms of polymorphism (compile-time overloading vs runtime overriding), abstract classes vs interfaces (and the critical 'when would you choose each?' question), and constructors including default, parameterised, and copy constructors. The 'this' and 'super' keywords appear in almost every OOP answer and are explained here with runnable examples. Every answer ends with the meta-signal — what the interviewer is checking beyond the surface question.

modules.title: Java Strings & Wrapper Classes
modules.intro: String interview questions appear in every single Java fresher interview — often more than OOP questions. The reason is that strings expose memory (the String pool and why String is immutable), common programming mistakes (== vs .equals()), and practical skills (reverse a string, check palindrome, count character frequency). This module covers: why String is immutable in Java and the memory implications (String pool vs heap), the difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer (mutability, thread-safety, and when to choose each), the most-asked String methods (substring, charAt, indexOf, split, trim, contains, replace), and the string programs that show up in almost every fresher coding round. Wrapper classes and autoboxing/unboxing are included here because they appear alongside string and int conversion questions. Every code block runs standalone so you can copy-paste into your IDE.

modules.title: Java Collections Framework
modules.intro: Collections framework questions are in the top-three most asked topics in Java fresher interviews, right after OOP and strings. This module covers the Collections hierarchy (Collection → List/Set/Queue; Map is separate), every List implementation a fresher is expected to know (ArrayList vs LinkedList — what they are, when to use each, the performance difference), the most important Set types (HashSet vs TreeSet vs LinkedHashSet), and HashMap including how get/put works internally (hash codes, buckets, equals contract). The 'which collection would you use for X?' scenario appears in almost every interview and is answered with a decision table. Generics are introduced here because every collection uses them. The module ends with common iteration patterns (for-each, Iterator, Java 8 forEach) and the comparisons that always come up: List vs Set, HashMap vs Hashtable, fail-fast vs fail-safe.

modules.title: Java Exception Handling
modules.intro: Exception handling interview questions probe three things at once: your understanding of Java's type system (Throwable → Error vs Exception → checked vs unchecked), your practical skill (writing correct try-catch blocks, knowing when finally runs), and your design sense (when to create a custom exception vs wrap an existing one). This module covers: the full exception hierarchy with a visual — Throwable, Error, Exception, RuntimeException; the checked vs unchecked distinction and why it matters for method signatures (throws keyword); try, catch, finally, and the less-asked but high-signal try-with-resources; the difference between throw and throws; how to write a custom exception class and when that is the right design; and the common runtime exceptions every fresher must be able to explain (NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ClassCastException, NumberFormatException). Every answer ends with the meta-signal so you know what depth the interviewer wants.

modules.title: Java Multithreading Basics
modules.intro: Multithreading interview questions come up in almost every Java fresher interview even though most freshers have never written production multi-threaded code. Interviewers ask because the answers reveal whether you understand the JVM's execution model. This module is calibrated for freshers: it covers what a thread is versus a process, the two ways to create a thread in Java (extending Thread vs implementing Runnable — with the tradeoff that matters in interviews), the thread lifecycle (NEW → RUNNABLE → BLOCKED → WAITING → TERMINATED), why synchronization exists (race conditions), how synchronized works at the method and block level, the wait/notify contract, and the volatile keyword. The module deliberately stops before java.util.concurrent (that is intermediate territory) — freshers are expected to know the fundamentals without executor services or lock objects. Each code block is a complete runnable program so every concept is immediately testable.

modules.title: Java 8 Features for Freshers
modules.intro: Java 8 interview questions are now standard in every Java fresher interview — companies expect you to know lambdas and streams even for entry-level roles. This module covers: what a lambda expression is and the syntax (parameter list, arrow token, body), the four built-in functional interfaces every fresher must know (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier), how to use the Stream API for the operations interviewers probe (filter, map, collect, sorted, distinct, count, findFirst), what an Optional is and why it exists (avoiding NullPointerException), default and static methods in interfaces and why Java 8 added them, and method references as shorthand for lambdas. The module focuses on interview-level fluency — you do not need to understand parallel streams or collectors in depth at fresher level, but you must be able to write a 3-step stream pipeline and explain what each step does. Every code block has a main method you can run.

modules.title: Java I/O & File Handling Basics
modules.intro: Java I/O interview questions test whether you understand the layered stream model and when to use byte streams versus character streams. This module is scoped to what freshers are actually asked: the difference between InputStream/OutputStream and Reader/Writer (bytes vs characters), why BufferedReader/BufferedWriter exist (performance), the File class for path operations (exists, isDirectory, listFiles), serialization and why an object needs to implement Serializable, the try-with-resources pattern applied to streams (which every interviewer who asks about exceptions will follow up with), and a brief intro to the java.nio.file.Path/Files API that replaced much of java.io.File in modern Java. I/O questions are less frequent in fresher interviews than OOP or collections, but when asked they tend to be practical — 'how would you read a file line by line?' — so runnable examples are provided for every key pattern.

modules.title: Spring Boot for Freshers
modules.intro: Spring Boot interview questions are the most searched fresher topic alongside core Java because almost every Java backend job posting mentions Spring Boot. This module answers the questions that come up in every fresher screening: what is Spring Boot and how is it different from Spring Framework (auto-configuration, opinionated defaults, embedded server), what is a Spring Boot starter and why it simplifies dependency management, how the embedded Tomcat works and why it matters, what application.properties configures, and how to write a minimal REST controller (@RestController, @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @RequestBody, @PathVariable). The auto-configuration question — 'how does Spring Boot know which beans to create?' — is answered with the @EnableAutoConfiguration and spring.factories mechanism at a level appropriate for freshers. Every code example builds toward a working Hello World REST API you can run from your IDE.

modules.title: Spring Core & Dependency Injection
modules.intro: Spring Core interview questions probe the design pattern behind Spring: Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection (DI). These questions come up in two contexts — standalone 'explain DI' questions and follow-ups after a Spring Boot question. This module covers: what IoC means (the framework controls object creation, not you), what DI means (dependencies are injected rather than created inside the class), the three forms of DI (constructor injection, setter injection, field injection) with the tradeoffs the interviewer is listening for (constructor is preferred for required dependencies), the Spring IoC container and ApplicationContext, how @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller differ (and the answer is: they are all @Component specialisations with semantic meaning and AOP hooks), bean scopes (singleton vs prototype at a minimum), and the @Autowired annotation. Every concept is illustrated with a runnable Spring Boot example that a fresher can copy into their project.

modules.title: Spring Data JPA Basics
modules.intro: Spring Data JPA interview questions are asked in nearly every Java backend fresher interview because they combine two topics at once: the ORM concept (how Java objects map to database tables) and the Spring Data abstraction (how JPA Repository eliminates boilerplate DAO code). This module covers: what JPA is and the role of Hibernate as the JPA provider, the core annotations every fresher must know (@Entity, @Table, @Id, @GeneratedValue, @Column), how to declare a JpaRepository or CrudRepository and get CRUD operations for free, Spring Data's derived query method naming convention (findByEmailAndActive), basic entity relationships (@OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany with @JoinColumn), and the lazy vs eager loading distinction that appears in nearly every follow-up. The module stays at fresher depth — no JPQL queries, no Criteria API, no custom specifications. Those belong to the intermediate level.

modules.title: SQL Fundamentals
modules.intro: SQL interview questions are mandatory in every backend fresher interview regardless of the tech stack, because every backend application reads and writes a database. This module covers the SQL topics that come up most often for freshers: the DDL/DML/DQL classification (CREATE/INSERT/SELECT and why the distinction matters), writing SELECT queries with WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT, all four types of JOINs (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER) with a visual example for each, aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) with GROUP BY and HAVING, subqueries vs joins (when each is appropriate), basic index concepts (what an index is, why it speeds up reads but slows writes), and the key constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, DEFAULT). Every answer includes a short SQL snippet that runs against a simple two-table schema (users and orders) so all examples share consistent context.

modules.title: JDBC Fundamentals
modules.intro: JDBC interview questions test whether you understand how Java talks to a relational database at the low level — before any ORM or Spring Data abstraction. Many freshers have only used JPA and get caught by 'how does Spring Data work under the hood?'. This module covers: the JDBC API architecture (DriverManager, Connection, Statement, ResultSet), the JDBC connection flow (load driver, get connection, create statement, execute, read result, close), the three statement types (Statement, PreparedStatement, CallableStatement) and why PreparedStatement is almost always the right choice (parameterised queries, SQL injection prevention, performance), how to iterate a ResultSet, what connection pooling is and why it exists (HikariCP is the default in Spring Boot), and the JDBC vs JPA comparison that appears in almost every data-layer discussion. SQL injection via Statement concatenation is shown explicitly here because understanding the problem makes PreparedStatement's value immediately clear.

modules.title: Database Design Basics
modules.intro: Database design interview questions test whether you can think beyond writing queries to designing a schema that is correct, maintainable, and efficient. Freshers are expected to know the basics: 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF normalization (what each form eliminates, with a before-and-after table example), primary keys and foreign keys (the difference and the referential integrity constraint), ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the 'D' in ACID is the one most freshers miss), what a transaction is and the commit/rollback model, how to read and sketch a basic entity-relationship (ER) diagram, and the relational vs NoSQL comparison at a conceptual level (structured vs unstructured, schema-on-write vs schema-on-read, when each fits). The 'what is ACID?' question is one of the most asked data-layer questions in fresher interviews and the answer here is structured so each property is memorable with a one-sentence definition and a one-sentence failure scenario.

modules.title: REST API Fundamentals
modules.intro: REST API interview questions are asked in every Java backend fresher interview because every modern backend is built around APIs. Interviewers use these questions to check two things: whether you understand the HTTP protocol (verbs, status codes, request/response structure) and whether you can design a clean URL scheme. This module covers: what REST means and the six architectural constraints (stateless and uniform interface are the two that come up most), the HTTP verbs and their semantic meanings (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE — with idempotency as the key differentiator), the status code groups (1xx/2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx) and the specific codes every fresher must know (200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500), JSON structure (objects, arrays, nesting — with the Java Jackson mapping), how to design RESTful URLs (nouns not verbs, plural resources, nested resources for relationships), and the REST vs SOAP comparison that occasionally appears. The module pairs directly with the Spring MVC & REST module that follows.

modules.title: Spring MVC & REST Controllers
modules.intro: Spring MVC interview questions test whether you can connect the REST concepts from the previous module to the Spring implementation. This module covers: the MVC pattern (Model-View-Controller) and how Spring MVC maps to it in a REST API (the 'View' is JSON, not HTML), the DispatcherServlet as the front-controller and the request processing chain, the annotation stack every fresher must know (@RestController vs @Controller, @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping), how to extract data from requests (@PathVariable for URL segments, @RequestParam for query parameters, @RequestBody for JSON), how to shape responses (ResponseEntity for explicit status codes and headers, @ResponseStatus), how Spring MVC handles errors (@ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler for global error handling), and what content negotiation means. Every code block builds toward a working three-endpoint CRUD controller for a simple resource.

modules.title: SOLID & OOP Design Principles
modules.intro: SOLID principles interview questions are asked in nearly every fresher interview because they separate candidates who understand design from candidates who only understand syntax. This module covers each SOLID principle at fresher level: Single Responsibility (one reason to change — the most violated principle in fresher code), Open/Closed (extend without modifying — the foundation of plugin architectures), Liskov Substitution (subclass must honour the parent contract — the principle behind the classic Rectangle/Square counterexample), Interface Segregation (clients should not be forced to implement interfaces they do not use), and Dependency Inversion (depend on abstractions, not concretions — the principle behind Spring DI). The other principles that appear alongside SOLID are covered too: DRY (Do not Repeat Yourself), KISS (Keep It Simple), YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It), composition vs inheritance, and the coupling/cohesion tradeoff. Every principle is illustrated with a before (violation) and after (fixed) code example.

modules.title: Design Patterns Introduction
modules.intro: Design patterns interview questions at fresher level test whether you know the vocabulary of software design — and whether you can connect patterns to real code you have written. This module covers the seven patterns that appear most in fresher interviews: Singleton (one instance, thread-safety concerns, double-checked locking), Factory/Abstract Factory (create objects without specifying the exact class, used everywhere in Spring), Builder (constructing complex objects step by step, the pattern behind StringBuilder and JPA CriteriaBuilder), Strategy (encapsulate interchangeable algorithms — sorting, payment methods), Observer (event/listener model — used in Spring Events and every UI framework), and Decorator (add behaviour without modifying the class — used in Java I/O streams). The 'when to use patterns' question is included explicitly because interviewers test judgment, not just recognition. Each pattern has a Java code example of ≤20 lines and a 'where you see it in the JDK or Spring' anchor.

modules.title: Low-Level Design (LLD) Basics
modules.intro: Low-Level Design (LLD) interview questions have entered fresher interviews at product companies (think Flipkart, Swiggy, Zomato, Paytm). The interviewer gives you a real-world system — a parking lot, a library, an ATM — and asks you to design the classes, attributes, and methods. This module teaches a repeatable four-step approach: clarify requirements, identify entities (nouns become classes), identify relationships (is-a vs has-a), assign responsibilities to methods. The module covers four canonical LLD problems at fresher level: Parking Lot (classes: ParkingLot, Floor, Slot, Vehicle, Ticket), Library Management (Book, Member, Librarian, Loan, Fine), Online Shopping Cart (Product, Cart, Order, Payment), and ATM (Card, Account, ATM, Transaction). For each problem the module shows a class diagram sketch and the key design decisions to explain aloud. UML class diagram basics (box, arrow types) are introduced so you can communicate your design on a whiteboard.

modules.title: Data Structures & Algorithms for Interviews
modules.intro: Data structures and algorithms questions are present in the majority of fresher coding rounds at product companies. This module covers the DSA topics a Java fresher is expected to handle: Big-O complexity analysis (time and space — the language of every DSA discussion), arrays and strings (the most common interview substrate: two-pointer, sliding window, prefix sum), linked lists (reversing, detecting a cycle with Floyd's algorithm, finding the middle), stacks and queues (Java's Stack/Deque, balanced parentheses, next greater element), binary trees (traversals: inorder/preorder/postorder, height, level-order BFS), sorting algorithms (bubble, selection, insertion at concept level; merge sort and quicksort with complexity), binary search (on sorted arrays and the 'find first/last occurrence' variant), and hashing in interviews (using HashMap/HashSet to reduce O(n²) to O(n) — the pattern behind most medium problems). Every problem includes a Java solution with main method and a Big-O analysis.

modules.title: Interview Problem-Solving Patterns
modules.intro: Interview problem-solving pattern questions test whether you can recognise the algorithm category before starting to code — the skill that separates candidates who solve problems from candidates who stare at a blank screen. This module teaches the five patterns a fresher must internalise: Two Pointers (sorted array sum, remove duplicates, valid palindrome), Sliding Window (maximum subarray of size k, longest substring without repeating characters), Frequency Counting (anagram detection, find duplicate in array using HashMap), Recursion basics (factorial, Fibonacci — understanding the call stack and base case), and Dynamic Programming intro (the Fibonacci→memoisation transformation that every fresher should be able to code live). The interview approach framework is included: restate the problem, clarify edge cases, think out loud about brute force then optimise, code, trace through an example, state the complexity. Common fresher programs that appear as warm-up questions are covered (reverse a string, check prime, Fibonacci series, FizzBuzz, find second largest).

modules.title: Web Security for Freshers
modules.intro: Web security interview questions at fresher level focus on awareness and vocabulary rather than implementation depth. Interviewers check whether you know the common attacks and the standard defences — candidates who cannot name SQL injection or XSS raise a red flag even at entry level. This module covers: authentication (who are you?) vs authorisation (what can you do?), HTTPS and TLS at a conceptual level (certificate, handshake, why HTTP is insufficient), SQL injection (what it is, a live example against a vulnerable query, how PreparedStatement prevents it), Cross-Site Scripting XSS (reflected vs stored, how output encoding prevents it), CSRF (the attack model and the CSRF token defence), JWT (header.payload.signature structure, where to store it, stateless vs session-based auth), password hashing (why MD5/SHA1 are insufficient, bcrypt/Argon2 as the standard), and the OWASP Top 10 as a vocabulary list. Security questions at fresher level are worth preparing for because a correct answer in this area is a disproportionate differentiator.

modules.title: JUnit 5 & Unit Testing
modules.intro: JUnit interview questions test whether you can write and reason about automated tests — a skill that separates professional developers from script writers. Freshers often skip testing in college projects, so demonstrating testing knowledge is a differentiator. This module covers: what unit testing is and why it matters (fast feedback, documentation, regression safety), the JUnit 5 annotation model (@Test, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @BeforeAll, @AfterAll, @Disabled, @DisplayName), the assertion library (assertEquals, assertTrue, assertThrows, assertAll), how @ParameterizedTest with @ValueSource and @CsvSource eliminates repetitive test methods, the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern as a naming and structure discipline, what makes a good unit test (FIRST: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely), and the practical question 'what is hard to unit test and why?' (static methods, constructors, I/O, time — the answer leads naturally into Mockito). Every test in the module tests the same simple Calculator or BankAccount class so examples build on each other.

modules.title: Mockito & Test Doubles
modules.intro: Mockito interview questions are asked when the interviewer wants to know whether you can test a class that has dependencies — the real-world case where JUnit alone is insufficient. This module covers: what a test double is and the vocabulary (mock vs stub vs spy — a comparison table is provided because the terms are often confused), how to create a mock with @Mock and @InjectMocks (including the @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) setup), the when().thenReturn() pattern for stubbing return values, the verify() assertion for checking that a method was called (and how many times), argument matchers (any(), eq(), anyString() for flexible argument matching), spy vs mock (spy wraps real object; use when you only want to stub part of the behaviour), and how to test a Spring @Service in isolation by mocking its @Repository dependency. The module ends with 'what should you not mock?' — static methods, value objects, the class under test — because judgment is what interviewers are testing.

modules.title: Git Version Control
modules.intro: Git interview questions are asked in every fresher technical interview because version control is the first tool a developer uses on their first day. Interviewers check whether you have actually used Git in a team setting (college projects count) or just know it theoretically. This module covers: the Git data model (working directory → staging area → local repository → remote repository), the core commands every fresher must execute without thinking (git init, add, commit, push, pull, fetch, status, log, diff), branching (git branch, checkout, switch) and the 'why branch?' mental model, merging vs rebasing (the difference and when each is appropriate — merge for shared branches, rebase for feature branches is the pragmatic answer), resolving merge conflicts step by step, what a pull request is and the review workflow, and the Git workflows used in teams (feature branch workflow is the minimum; Gitflow as a named reference). Every command is shown with the exact syntax and a short explanation of what it does under the hood.

modules.title: Maven & Gradle Build Tools
modules.intro: Maven and Gradle interview questions test whether you understand how a Java project is compiled, tested, and packaged. Most freshers use these tools daily without understanding what they do — the ones who can explain what mvn package actually does stand out. This module covers: what a build tool is and why it exists (before Maven, Java projects were compiled by hand with classpath flags), the Maven project structure (src/main/java, src/test/java, target), the pom.xml structure (groupId/artifactId/version, dependencies, plugins), the Maven lifecycle phases and which commands trigger which phases (clean, compile, test, package, install, deploy), how dependency management works (Maven Central, transitive dependencies, dependency scope: compile vs test vs provided), Maven vs Gradle comparison (Gradle's incremental build and Kotlin DSL vs Maven's XML and convention-over-configuration), how to run a Spring Boot application with Maven (mvn spring-boot:run), and what a build profile is and when you need one (dev vs prod configuration). Gradle coverage is at concept level for freshers.

modules.title: Docker & Cloud Concepts Introduction
modules.intro: Docker and cloud interview questions have moved into fresher interviews at product companies as containerised deployments became the industry default. You are not expected to be a Docker expert at fresher level, but you must know the vocabulary and be able to explain the core concept. This module covers: what Docker is and what problem it solves (the 'works on my machine' problem), containers vs virtual machines (shared kernel vs full OS — the key difference and why containers start in milliseconds), Docker images vs containers (image is the blueprint, container is the running instance), a minimal Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application, the Docker commands every fresher should know (build, run, ps, stop, exec, logs, pull), docker-compose intro (running an app + database together), cloud computing fundamentals (on-premise vs cloud, the economics), IaaS/PaaS/SaaS with a real example for each, and microservices introduction at concept level (what they are, why they exist, monolith vs microservices tradeoffs at a high level). The depth here is intentionally fresher-appropriate — no Kubernetes, no EKS.

modules.title: Debugging, Logging & Code Quality
modules.intro: Debugging and logging interview questions test practical day-one skills. Interviewers ask these because they want to know whether you will be productive from the first week or will need constant hand-holding. This module covers: the debugging workflow (read the error message first, reproduce reliably, isolate the failing component, form a hypothesis, test it, fix it), how to use an IDE debugger (breakpoints, step over vs step into, watch expressions, evaluate expression — the five actions you need for 90% of bugs), what logging is for (production visibility when you cannot attach a debugger), log levels (TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR) and the rule for which level to use where (INFO for business events, WARN for recoverable issues, ERROR for failures that need attention), how SLF4J + Logback work in Spring Boot and why you use the SLF4J API not Logback directly (provider independence), how to read a stack trace (start at the top, find your code in the trace, read the exception message before the trace), the ten most common Java exceptions a fresher must be able to explain on sight, and what reviewers look for in a fresher's code (variable naming, method length, null handling, test coverage).

modules.title: Fresher Behavioral & HR Questions
modules.intro: Fresher behavioral and HR interview questions take up half of every entry-level interview — often more than the technical questions. Most candidates underprepare this section because it feels less technical, but a weak 'tell me about yourself' answer can end an interview faster than a wrong algorithm. This module covers every question that appears in fresher HR rounds: tell me about yourself (a structured 90-second answer template covering education, key skills, one project, and why this role), strengths and weaknesses (how to answer honestly without disqualifying yourself — the weakness answer is a skill you are actively improving), why this company (a three-part answer: the company's product, the team's tech stack, the growth opportunity you see for yourself), why Java backend (your story, not a generic answer), talking about a college or personal project (use STAR structure: Situation, Task, Action, Result, and include the tech stack), teamwork and conflict (how you handled a disagreement with a teammate), career goals (be honest about learning direction, not promotion timeline), and offer/salary negotiation basics for freshers.

modules.title: Technical Interview Preparation
modules.intro: Technical interview preparation questions are the meta-layer that ties every other module together. This module does not teach a new topic — it teaches how to perform what you already know under interview pressure. It covers: the five-step approach to a coding problem (read, clarify, brute force, optimise, code — out loud), how to handle whiteboard coding (think before writing, explain as you go, name your variables well), what to do when you do not know the answer (acknowledge gaps honestly, reason from first principles, show the interviewer your thinking process), the early system design questions that appear in fresher interviews at product companies ('design a URL shortener in 15 minutes'), the post-interview follow-up email (whether to send one and how to write it), how to run a mock interview with a peer, and the ten most common fresher mistakes (jumping to code before clarifying, not testing edge cases, saying 'I don't know' and stopping, speaking too quietly, not asking questions at the end).

modules.title: Spring Security Basics
modules.intro: Spring Security basics are asked in almost every Java fresher interview at a product company. This module covers the core concepts freshers are expected to know: the difference between authentication (who are you?) and authorization (what can you do?), how Spring Security's filter chain works, configuring HTTP security rules with SecurityFilterChain, JWT-based stateless auth (how a token is issued and validated), form-based login and session management, and @PreAuthorize for method-level access control. No deep dives — just enough to answer confidently without over-claiming.
